summary: Describes the MIME header Content-Duration for time-varying media like audio and video. It obsoletes RFC 2424.

eli5.summary: This adds a label saying how long a recording lasts, like the running time on a video.

subtitle: A one-line mail header that states how many seconds a voice or video attachment lasts.

tldr.problem: Audio and video attachments have a running time, but finding it normally means opening and decoding the content.
tldr.mechanism: The Content-Duration header field carries the length in seconds as a single number with no units, written as 1 to 10 digits.
tldr.outcome: A mail reader can show the duration without opening the media, but the value is only a sender's claim and must not be trusted to find the data size.

today: RFC 3803 is a Draft Standard published in June 2004. It obsoletes RFC 2424, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Header Is For
sections.content:
Time-varying media such as a spoken voice message or a video clip has an inherent duration. Many encodings store it internally or let you work it out from the byte length. Even so, it can be useful to put the duration in a MIME header so it is available without dealing with the content.

This document defines the Content-Duration header for any such content, typically audio/* or video/*. It obsoletes RFC 2424, and the only differences are editorial and boilerplate changes.
sections.eli5: Instead of playing a song to learn how long it is, you read the number written on the case.

sections.title: Syntax and Meaning
sections.content:
The value is a single number of seconds, with no units tag. The formal rule is duration := "Content-Duration" ":" 1*10DIGIT. In practice the upper bound is 2147483647, which is 2^31 - 1. An example is Content-Duration: 33, meaning 33 seconds.

The time value should be exact, but the exact figure cannot be known without playing the content. If an exact value is needed, playing it is the method to use. The header just lets a sender put a value in an easy place. How a receiver shows it, for example in the inbox or when the attachment is opened, is a local implementation issue.
sections.eli5: The number is a plain count of seconds, like 33. It is the sender's best answer, not a stopwatch reading.

sections.title: Use in Voice Mail
sections.content: The header is a useful part of the Voice Profile for Internet Mail version 2 (VPIM), defined in RFC 3801. All VPIM messages MUST contain the audio/32KADPCM sub-type to carry the audio of a voice message. Showing the duration helps, for instance, on a simple MIME or non-MIME desktop where opening the audio is awkward.
sections.eli5: Voice mail systems use it so you can see how long a message is before listening.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Putting the duration outside the binary data may be a security issue in some environments, though likely not most, and in those it should not be noted. The header cannot be trusted to determine the exact size of the data. The exact length must be found by examining the data itself.
sections.eli5: Do not believe the label when it matters. Check the real recording.
